charts.question: How have the yearly publication counts and venue shares changed across the IEEE VIS record?
charts.chart_title: Volume growth is tied to the changing conference mix

interaction.instruction: Click a conference in the legend to keep it prominent while the other venues fade.

charts.how_to_read: Each stacked bar is one year; total bar height is annual volume, and colored segments show how much each conference contributed within that year.
charts.summary: Annual volume ranges from 53 papers in 1990 to 174 papers in 2004, and in 2024 the largest conference group is Vis with 124 papers. The chart shows why counts and shares must be read together: the same annual total can come from very different venue mixes.

criteria.rationale: uses year-conference counts and shares
links volume to within-year mix
extends the stem from totals to composition
stacking supports whole-year totals but limits segment comparison
legend selection clearly changes emphasis

self_eval.weakest: Stacked bars make non-baseline conference trends harder to compare.

charts.question: When did the publication record shift from conference papers toward journal papers?
charts.chart_title: Journal papers dominate the record by 2024

interaction.instruction: Click C, J, or M in the legend to isolate that paper-type trajectory.

charts.how_to_read: Follow each paper-type line across years; the highest line in a year is the largest type share for that year.
charts.summary: By 2024, journal papers account for 100.0% of 124 papers, and across 1990–2024 the record contains 1,999 J papers versus 1,559 C papers and 319 M papers. The format shift is therefore not just an end-year anomaly; J is also the largest paper type over the full record.

criteria.rationale: uses paper-type shares and totals directly
connects annual endpoint with full-record totals
delivers the stem’s main pivot
line chart fits share trajectories
legend highlight helps but does not compute crossover

self_eval.weakest: It shows the transition visually but the summary can only state the supported endpoint and totals.

charts.question: Did collaboration size and keyword coverage rise alongside the publication-format shift?
charts.chart_title: Collaboration and keyword coverage both rise by 2024

interaction.instruction: Move the Through year slider backward to test whether the authorship–keyword pattern is driven by the latest years.

charts.how_to_read: The path connects years in order; movement up means broader keyword coverage, and movement right means larger author teams.
charts.summary: Average authors per paper rises from 2.2642 in 1990 to 4.7016 in 2024, while keyword coverage reaches 100.0% in 2024. This supports a parallel maturation story—larger collaborations and more complete keyword metadata accompany the publication-format shift, but this panel does not prove causation.

criteria.rationale: endpoint values match the authorship-keyword aggregate
states the parallel rise and causal limit
extends the stem into metadata maturation
connected scatter fits two-measure change over time
year slider visibly shortens the path

self_eval.weakest: The chart implies temporal association, not a formal model.

charts.question: How many papers were published each year?
charts.chart_title: Annual VIS output ranges from 53 to 174 papers

interaction.instruction: Move the Start year slider to focus the line on later parts of the 1990–2024 record.

charts.how_to_read: Read left to right: each point is one publication year, and higher points mean more papers that year.
charts.summary: From 1990 through 2024, IEEE VIS yearly output ranges from 53 papers in 1990 to 174 papers in 2004, within a 3,877-paper record. Treat the peak as an annual-volume high, not as evidence of paper type or venue mix by itself.

criteria.rationale: uses the per-year count table directly
names range and peak year
opens the volume story cleanly
line fits ordered yearly counts
range filter visibly changes the years shown

self_eval.weakest: It answers volume only, leaving composition to later panels.

charts.question: Which conference contributed the most papers overall?
charts.chart_title: Vis contributes the largest overall paper count

interaction.instruction: Raise the Minimum papers slider to leave only conferences above that threshold.

charts.how_to_read: The longest bar is the conference with the most papers across the full 1990–2024 record.
charts.summary: Vis contributed the most papers overall, with 1,942 of the 3,877 papers in the record. That makes venue mix central: the total growth is not evenly distributed across the named conferences.

criteria.rationale: counts come from the conference aggregate
turns ranking into a venue-mix implication
connects volume to venue concentration
ranked horizontal bars suit four conferences
threshold filter visibly removes bars

self_eval.weakest: It does not show when the venue concentration emerges.

charts.question: When did journal papers become the main kind of paper?
charts.chart_title: Journal is the main paper kind by 2024

interaction.instruction: Use the dropdown to switch from Journal (J) to Conference (C) or Misc. (M) and see which years each kind led.

charts.how_to_read: In the default view, each point is a year when journal papers were the largest paper kind; higher points mean journals made up more of that year’s papers.
charts.summary: In the default Journal (J) view, 2024 is a journal-led year with 124 J papers, or 100.0% of that year’s publications. Switch the dropdown to C or M to compare which years were led by conference or miscellaneous papers instead.

criteria.rationale: winner filter uses within-year max share
locates leadership years rather than all shares
turns the main shift into reader exploration
point strip is simple for locating years
dropdown is useful but hides other types at once

self_eval.weakest: It requires interaction to compare all paper kinds.
